findings.issue_text: [BUG] submit() now calls record_stored_segments() on every shard buffer on every message, multiplying Redis round-trips by the number of flusher processes. The consumer hot path performs num_processes Redis calls (each with its own connection from a separately-constructed SpansBuffer) per submit instead of one; with the CLI default flusher_processes=1 this is neutral, but any operator raising --flusher-processes gets a linear Redis load increase on the exact path the old code kept at one call, and record_stored_segments is now called on buffers whose processes also flush concurrently — the Redis memory/CPU cost of the flusher subsystem scales superlinearly with shard count under load.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code — no call site anywhere in the diff or its comment's stated purpose is unreachable. Next maintainer changing shard assignment or restart logic must reason about (or 'fix') a method that is never invoked; it duplicates _create_process_for_shards behavior with subtly different semantics (restarts by shard lookup vs. by index), which will mislead debugging of the restart path.

[ADVISORY] join() computes remaining_time but never uses it, leaving a dead variable that masks that the loop's real deadline logic is the duplicated check inside the inner while. The next change to shutdown timing (e.g., per-process timeout budgeting, which the variable name implies was intended) will build on a variable that does nothing; delete it or implement per-process timeout allocation.

[BUG] When produce_to_pipe is set (the thread mode used in every test and in single-process deployments), _ensure_processes_alive() detects an unhealthy 'process' (a threading.Thread) but process.kill() is skipped by the isinstance check, so the hung thread keeps running while _create_process_for_shards spawns a second thread flushing the same shards against a fresh SpansBuffer. Two threads now concurrently poll and flush the same shard set; the old code had the same kill limitation but created a single replacement only after the consumer restarted — here the restart counter resets nothing and the duplicate thread accumulates every max-unhealthy-seconds interval until MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS raises RuntimeError, during which spans are produced to the pipe/Kafka twice or torn between two buffers whose record_stored_segments state diverges.

[ADVISORY] The metric tag key is "shards" in the wait_produce timer but "shard" in the produce timer and flusher_unhealthy counter, so the same shard dimension lands under two tag names. Anyone building dashboards/alerts on spans.buffer.flusher metrics after this diff gets split series for the identical dimension; fixing it later renames history. Rebuttal ("just a typo") fails because metric tag renames are permanent cardinality/history decisions, and the diff introduces the inconsistency itself.

[ADVISORY] Per-process bookkeeping (process_healthy_since, process_backpressure_since, process_restarts, buffers, processes, process_to_shards_map) is six parallel hand-maintained dicts keyed by process_index whose consistency is enforced only by convention. The next change (e.g., resharding on rebalance, which the process_to_shards_map comment implies is coming) must update all six dicts in lockstep or KeyError at runtime; a single dataclass/record per process (holding process, buffer, shards, and shared Values) would collapse the alignment burden and delete the index-plumbing in _create_process_for_shards and _ensure_processes_alive.

[ADVISORY] test_basic now depends on a real time.sleep(0.1) to wait for flusher threads, a flaky timing hack replacing deterministic synchronization. CI intermittently fails (or, worse, silently passes without the flusher completing) on slow runners; the new test_flusher_processes_limit has the same shape (asserts on thread/process creation only, never on flushing behavior under the limit), so the max_processes code path's actual flush behavior has no coverage — a regression that distributes shards wrongly or double-flushes will not fail either test.

[BUG] The health-monitoring/restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive` — crash-restart, hang detection via `process_healthy_since`, the per-process `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` RuntimeError, and per-shard `flusher_unhealthy` metric tagging — has no test anywhere in the diff, even though it is the PR's headline feature. A regression in restart accounting (e.g. the per-process restart counter or the kill/respawn of a shard group) ships silently and is only discovered in production when a hung flusher process is never restarted, Redis fills past the memory threshold, and the consumer stops making progress with no alert.

[BUG] `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` produces 0 processes when `assigned_shards` is empty, leaving the flusher with no processes and no monitoring of anything, and the `max_processes or len(...)` expression maps `flusher_processes=0` to 'one process per shard' instead of rejecting it. An operator setting `--flusher-processes 0` on the CLI (or a code path passing 0) gets the opposite of the intended limit — a full per-shard process fleet — with no error, and an empty-shard rebalance leaves the flusher structurally inert while the consumer keeps accepting messages.

[ADVISORY] The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` while every other metric on the same path (`flusher.produce`, `segment_size_bytes`, `flusher_unhealthy`, `flusher.backpressure`) uses the singular key `"shard"`, splitting the same shard dimension across two tag names. Whoever builds dashboards/alerts on flusher shard granularity (SRE on-call during a partial-shard backlog) gets two disjoint series and silently misses wait_produce data when filtering by the `shard` tag used everywhere else.

[ADVISORY] The Redis memory check now sums `used` and `available` across every per-shard `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` result, double-counting host-level Redis memory once per process-owned buffer when multiple buffers report on the same Redis service. With `max_memory_percentage < 1.0`, the computed `used/available` ratio is skewed by the number of flusher processes, so a high `--flusher-processes` value makes the consumer trip `MessageRejected` (or fail to trip it) based on process count rather than actual Redis memory; no test covers multi-buffer aggregation.

[ADVISORY] `join()` breaks out of the per-process loop as soon as the deadline expires, skipping `terminate()` on all remaining processes, and the `test_flusher_processes_limit` test never exercises `join()` with a timeout or a still-alive process. A consumer shutdown under a hung flusher process leaks that process past the deadline; because processes are daemon=True this is masked in normal operation but bites in tests and embedded deployments where the parent outlives the consumer.

[ADVISORY] This PR adds an unrelated Python style-guide example (hasattr vs isinstance for unions) to CLAUDE.md, which is not traceable to the span buffer multiprocess/health-monitoring intent. Doc maintainers get out-of-scope churn mixed into a behavioral PR, making the diff harder to review and bisect; nothing in the PR title or description justifies it.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code — no caller anywhere in the diff or existing code invokes it, since restarts go through _ensure_processes_alive calling _create_process_for_shards directly. Future maintainers may call it for a single-shard restart and silently create a duplicate process for the whole shard group (it re-creates the full multi-shard process), violating the single-writer-per-process invariant the mapping is supposed to enforce.

[ADVISORY] The wait_produce timer uses the tag key "shards" while the produce timer and segment_size timing use the tag key "shard", so the same logical dimension is emitted under two different tag keys. Dashboards/alerts keyed on spans.buffer.flusher.* with tag shard will silently miss the wait_produce series (and vice versa), splitting the health-monitoring view the PR is supposed to provide.

[ADVISORY] The backpressure metric and MessageRejected check now emit spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure once per backpressured process rather than once per submit, so the counter is inflated by a factor equal to the number of processes under backpressure. Anyone alerting on the existing backpressure metric sees a step-change in volume after this deploy (N processes -> up to N increments per rejected message), polluting trend baselines with no accompanying requirement.

[ADVISORY] The comment 'Update healthy_since for all shards handled by this process' is inaccurate — healthy_since is a single per-process Value, not a per-shard value, so the comment describes an invariant the code does not implement. A maintainer debugging shard-level health will read this comment and assume per-shard health tracking exists, sending them down a wrong debugging path in a codebase whose whole purpose here is health monitoring.

[ADVISORY] self.buffer is dropped entirely (each process builds its own SpansBuffer(shards)), but submit() now calls buffer.record_stored_segments() on every shard buffer on every message, a behavior change from the single call on the original buffer that is not covered by any test asserting the recording semantics. If record_stored_segments is a global counter (e.g. Redis INCR over the buffer's namespace) rather than shard-scoped, it is now incremented N times per message, skewing the drift calculation and any operator dashboard built on it; no test in the diff pins this down.

[BUG] The single-shard restart helper `_create_process_for_shard` restarts a process without killing the existing one, so a hung process plus its replacement both flush the same shards concurrently, producing duplicate span segments to Kafka. If any caller uses this path (it is currently dead code, which is itself misleading), a hung-but-alive process keeps polling Redis for the same shards while the new process flushes them too, double-producing every segment; consumers see each span batch twice.

[BUG] In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the `process.kill()` is skipped for `threading.Thread` instances (guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`), so in pipe/test mode a hung thread is never stopped before `_create_process_for_shards` spawns a replacement for the same shards. Whenever `produce_to_pipe` is set (tests, embedded mode) and a flusher thread hangs past `max-unhealthy-seconds`, the restart spawns a second thread flushing the identical shard set: duplicate payloads in the pipe and duplicated test messages, plus an unbounded leak of hung threads on repeated restarts.

[ADVISORY] `submit()` now calls `buffer.record_stored_segments()` and `buffer.get_memory_info()` once per per-shard buffer on every submit, turning what was one Redis interaction into N (one per flusher process) per consumed message batch. Operators running many flusher processes multiply the Redis round-trips per submit and multiply the number of Redis connection pools (one per SpansBuffer created in `_create_process_for_shards`), increasing Redis load and connection count exactly on the path meant to shed load; the memory-percentage check also sums `available` across N buffers that may report the same host memory N times, skewing the used/available ratio toward triggering backpressure.

[ADVISORY] `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats `0` as "unlimited" and makes the semantics of the new `--flusher-processes` CLI flag ambiguous against the `None` default, which already means one-process-per-shard. An operator setting `--flusher-processes 0` expecting to disable the flusher gets the maximum process fan-out instead, and the CLI help text ("Maximum number of processes... Defaults to 1") does not match the factory default (None → one process per shard), so the next deploy-tuning change gets silently wrong process counts.

[ADVISORY] `join()` breaks out of the per-process loop when the deadline expires, so any processes after the current index are neither waited on nor terminated, and their terminate is skipped entirely. On shutdown with a tight timeout and multiple flusher processes, later processes are left running (daemon flag saves the parent exit, but any graceful-shutdown invariants like flushing pending segments apply only to the first process in iteration order); during consumer restarts triggered by the RuntimeError path this can leave orphaned spawn processes holding Redis subscriptions briefly.

[ADVISORY] The metric tag key is inconsistent within the same diff: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` while `wait_produce` uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}`, splitting the same logical dimension across two tag names. Anyone building dashboards over flusher timing by shard must query two different tag keys depending on the metric, and any aggregation joining them silently drops data; the next editor copying one of the two lines propagates the split further.

[ADVISORY] The new multiprocess restart/unhealthy logic (`_ensure_processes_alive` hang detection, per-process restart counting, RuntimeError after MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS, and the thread-mode kill skip) has no test coverage in the diff; the new test only asserts process-count bookkeeping. The highest-risk behavior of this change — what happens when a flusher process hangs or dies with multiple processes sharing shards — ships unverified; a regression in the restart path (e.g. the thread-kill skip) would pass CI while duplicating or dropping spans in production.

[BUG] The default behavior silently changed from one flusher process to one process per shard: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` makes `flusher_processes=None` (the factory default, used by every construction path other than the new CLI option) spawn `len(assigned_shards)` processes. Any deployment or test constructing ProcessSpansStrategyFactory without passing flusher_processes (including the existing `ingest-transactions` consumer where the new --flusher-processes option is added, but any other factory call site) goes from 1 flusher process to N processes per consumer instance on upgrade, multiplying Redis connections, memory, and spawn overhead with no operator acceptance — the CLI default of 1 does not match the library default of all-shards.

[ADVISORY] `join()` breaks out of the whole process loop when the deadline expires, so remaining processes never reach the `process.terminate()` call that the previous single-process implementation always executed after the wait loop. On shutdown with a short join timeout and multiple flusher processes, processes after the current one in dict order are left running (daemon-terminated eventually, but potentially after producing duplicate segments or holding Redis locks longer than the old design guaranteed) — operators relying on the old guaranteed terminate-after-timeout invariant get orphaned workers during shutdown.

[ADVISORY] The memory backpressure check now sums `used`/`available` across all per-shard buffers via `memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` for each buffer, double-counting any service that appears in multiple buffers' get_memory_info results (the same Redis service serving all shards). When max_memory_percentage is configured below 1.0 and multiple flusher buffers report the same backing service, `used / available` is inflated by the number of buffers, tripping the `MessageRejected` memory backpressure far earlier than the accepted threshold — consumers stall on healthy Redis.

[ADVISORY] Metric tags are inconsistent across the new instrumentation: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use tag key `shard` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `shards` (and the value is a comma-joined multi-shard string rather than a single shard id, exploding tag cardinality per process restart as shard groupings change). Whoever builds dashboards/alerts on flusher per-shard metrics gets two disjoint tag keys for the same dimension, and the joined-string values (e.g. '3,7,11') prevent per-shard aggregation entirely; the existing `flusher_unhealthy` metric's shard tag is a plain int while produce's is a joined string, so the same shard is reported under different tag values.

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is dead code — no call site in the diff or existing code invokes it; restart logic uses `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) via `_ensure_processes_alive`. The next maintainer touching restart logic finds two near-duplicate process-creation entry points and picks the dead one, which does not update `self.processes[process_index]` bookkeeping in the restart path it implies (it re-creates without killing or replacing the tracked handle correctly for the multi-restart counter), making the change riskier.

[ADVISORY] `submit()` now calls `record_stored_segments()` on each per-shard buffer inside a Python loop on every submit, replacing a single call on the shared buffer, and the same pattern repeats for `get_memory_info()` — each call makes its own Redis round trip per buffer. Consumers with many shards and `max_processes` set high now perform N Redis calls (record_stored_segments, plus N more for memory info when memory backpressure is enabled) per submit where the accepted design performed one, reintroducing per-message Redis latency that the original single-buffer design explicitly avoided.

[ADVISORY] The test was changed from `@pytest.mark.django_db` to `@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)` and an unconditional `time.sleep(0.1)` was added after a bare `step.poll()` with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' — a test-only accommodation of the new multi-thread timing that the original synchronous-flush test did not need. The test now asserts the end-to-end message contents after a fixed 100ms sleep against background flusher threads, so CI intermittently fails (or silently passes with partially-flushed state) whenever thread scheduling exceeds the sleep; the next engineer debugging this flake cannot tell whether the flusher is broken or the sleep is too short, and the drift-change accompaniment masks real ordering regressions.

[BUG] The added `time.sleep(0.1)` in test_basic is a no-op because the same test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at its start, so the 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' wait never actually waits. The fix for the drift-change race is illusory: the flusher threads get zero wall-clock time before step.join(), so the test still races with the background threads and intermittently fails or (worse) passes without actually exercising the post-drift flush, giving false confidence that the timing change was tested.

[ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts internal bookkeeping (`len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes == 2`, `num_processes == 2`, shard-count sum) and never verifies that the two processes actually flush the data assigned to their shards. A regression where per-shard buffers are mis-wired (e.g. the round-robin process_to_shards_map assigns a shard to a process whose SpansBuffer(shards) excludes it, or a shared process never polls its second shard's Redis keys) passes this test, because no message flows through any of the 4 partitions — the test is a mirror of the constructor's arithmetic, not of flushing behavior. I checked tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py and test_flusher.py: neither asserts per-process or per-shard output when flusher_processes < shard count.

[BUG] test_flusher_processes_limit ends with a bare `step.join()` and never asserts any flushed messages or commits, so it cannot detect that the 2 shared processes fail to produce the segments written by submit(). If the refactor from one buffer to N per-shard SpansBuffer instances breaks data flow for shared processes (e.g. record_stored_segments on shard buffers that the flusher processes never read), the test still passes green, shipping a silent data-loss regression in span ingestion. The `messages` list captured via produce_to_pipe is never inspected.

[ADVISORY] The new restart/health logic in _ensure_processes_alive (per-process hang detection via process_healthy_since, process crash via is_alive/exitcode, the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError, and the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)-guarded kill) has no test in this diff that triggers any of these branches — both modified test files (test_consumer.py, test_flusher.py) only exercise the happy healthy path. The most safety-critical behavioral changes of the PR — kill/restart of a shared process, the AttributeError catch on killing a threading.Thread path, and the repeated-crash consumer restart — are unverified; a bug there (e.g. restart counter reset, wrong shared-state Value passed on recreate) ships silently and only surfaces as a hung or crash-looping production consumer.

[ADVISORY] The assertion was weakened from a specific `flusher.backpressure_since.value` check to `any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())`, which passes when only one of several per-process backpressure flags is set. In this multiprocess design the test now masks the case where some shard-processes never register backpressure that the old single-process code would have caught (e.g. a shared process whose backpressure Value is mis-wired in _create_process_for_shards); the test also never asserts the process_backpressure_since values belong to the processes actually owning the shards under load.

[BUG] A hung flusher running as a threading.Thread (the produce_to_pipe/test path) is never terminated on restart, so a duplicate flusher thread polls the same shards as the freshly spawned replacement. When the 'hang' path fires for a thread-based flusher, the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard skips the kill, _create_process_for_shards starts a second thread over the same shards; if the hung thread recovers, both threads consume the same Redis segments and produce duplicate span payloads to Kafka.

[ADVISORY] max_processes uses `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so flusher_processes=0 (or any falsy value) silently expands to one process per shard instead of being rejected or clamped. An operator setting --flusher-processes 0 via the new click option gets the maximum process count on a consumer with thousands of shards, multiplying spawn/Redis connection load with no error signal; the config value is silently ignored rather than validated.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code (no call sites in the diff) and, if ever wired up, would spawn a new process for a shard's group without killing the existing process stored in self.processes[process_index], leaking a live process that still flushes those shards. The next maintainer who fixes a rebalance bug by calling this method gets overlapping processes double-flushing the same shards; the deletion test passes — removing the method removes a future duplicate-data hazard.

[BUG] `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats an explicit `flusher_processes=0` as unset and silently falls back to one process per shard. An operator who sets --flusher-processes 0 intending to disable/limit the flusher instead gets the maximum fan-out (one spawn process per shard), the exact opposite of the requested limit, with no warning logged.

[BUG] When a hung flusher is running as a threading.Thread (produce_to_pipe mode), the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard means the hung thread is never killed before a replacement thread is spawned for the same shards. Two threads concurrently flush the same Redis shards, producing duplicate span batches to Kafka while the health monitor reports the flusher as recovered — silent data duplication with no error surfaced.

[ADVISORY] In join(), once the deadline is exhausted the `break` skips the terminate() call for all not-yet-iterated processes, leaving spawned flusher processes running past the consumer shutdown deadline. During a slow shutdown with a short join timeout, multiple non-daemon-joined flusher processes linger and keep polling Redis/producing to Kafka while the consumer is reported as shut down; behavior gets worse as flusher_processes grows since each process gets a fresh slice of the deadline.

[ADVISORY] When flusher_processes is None (any programmatic caller of ProcessSpansStrategyFactory that doesn't pass the new kwarg), the default silently changes from 1 shared flusher process to one process per shard. Any existing deployment/tooling that constructs the factory without --flusher-processes via the click option (tests, internal scripts) now spawns len(assigned_shards) processes instead of 1, multiplying Redis connections and memory with no operator action.

[ADVISORY] The metrics timers use inconsistent tag keys: 'shard' for spans.buffer.flusher.produce and segment_size_bytes, but 'shards' for spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce. Anyone debugging shard-level flusher latency in the metrics dashboard cannot join wait_produce with produce/segment_size metrics — the tag mismatch silently splits the series and misdirects investigation of slow flushes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] submit() now calls record_stored_segments() on every shard buffer on every message, multiplying Redis round-trips by the number of flusher processes. The consumer hot path performs num_processes Redis calls (each with its own connection from a separately-constructed SpansBuffer) per submit instead of one; with the CLI default flusher_processes=1 this is neutral, but any operator raising --flusher-processes gets a linear Redis load increase on the exact path the old code kept at one call, and record_stored_segments is now called on buffers whose processes also flush concurrently — the Redis memory/CPU cost of the flusher subsystem scales superlinearly with shard count under load.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `SpanFlusher.submit()` from a single call `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()` to looping over `self.buffers.values()` and calling `record_stored_segments()` on each (see `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): buffer.record_stored_segments()`). Since `_create_process_for_shards` now constructs a separate `SpansBuffer(shards)` per process and stores them in `self.buffers`, `submit()` will perform one `record_stored_segments()` call per flusher process (and thus per separately-constructed buffer) on every message. The finding’s core claim of linear increase in Redis work on the submit path when `--flusher-processes` is raised is grounded in the diff, but it’s a performance/scaling concern rather than a clear correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The memory backpressure check now sums `used`/`available` across all per-shard buffers via `memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` for each buffer, double-counting any service that appears in multiple buffers' get_memory_info results (the same Redis service serving all shards). When max_memory_percentage is configured below 1.0 and multiple flusher buffers report the same backing service, `used / available` is inflated by the number of buffers, tripping the `MessageRejected` memory backpressure far earlier than the accepted threshold — consumers stall on healthy Redis.

adjudication.rationale: In SpanFlusher.submit(), the memory backpressure calculation changed from a single buffer (`list(self.buffer.get_memory_info())`) to aggregating across all per-process buffers (`for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())`), then summing `used` and `available`. If multiple `SpansBuffer` instances report memory for the same backing service (e.g., the same Redis instance serving multiple shards), this aggregation will count that service multiple times, inflating `used/available` and potentially triggering `MessageRejected` earlier than intended. This risk is introduced by the diff’s move to one buffer per shard-group plus naive summation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Metric tags are inconsistent across the new instrumentation: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use tag key `shard` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `shards` (and the value is a comma-joined multi-shard string rather than a single shard id, exploding tag cardinality per process restart as shard groupings change). Whoever builds dashboards/alerts on flusher per-shard metrics gets two disjoint tag keys for the same dimension, and the joined-string values (e.g. '3,7,11') prevent per-shard aggregation entirely; the existing `flusher_unhealthy` metric's shard tag is a plain int while produce's is a joined string, so the same shard is reported under different tag values.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows inconsistent metric tag keys/values: in `SpanFlusher.main`, `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag})` and `metrics.timing("spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes", ..., tags={"shard": shard_tag})` use key `shard`, while `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag})` uses key `shards`. Also `shard_tag` is defined as `",".join(map(str, shards))`, so the value is a multi-shard string (e.g. "3,7") rather than a single shard id, whereas `_ensure_processes_alive` emits `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` with `tags={"cause": cause, "shard": shard}` where `shard` is an int. This is a concrete observability/instrumentation issue grounded in the diff, but it doesn’t directly break runtime correctness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is dead code — no call site in the diff or existing code invokes it; restart logic uses `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) via `_ensure_processes_alive`. The next maintainer touching restart logic finds two near-duplicate process-creation entry points and picks the dead one, which does not update `self.processes[process_index]` bookkeeping in the restart path it implies (it re-creates without killing or replacing the tracked handle correctly for the multi-restart counter), making the change riskier.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher` the method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is newly added, but the diff shows no call site for it; restart logic in `submit()` goes through `_ensure_processes_alive()` which restarts via `_create_process_for_shards(...)`. That makes `_create_process_for_shard` effectively dead/unused in this change and adds a confusing second entry point for restart/creation. While not a functional defect by itself, it is a diff-grounded maintainability risk (duplicate-looking APIs around process restart).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `submit()` now calls `record_stored_segments()` on each per-shard buffer inside a Python loop on every submit, replacing a single call on the shared buffer, and the same pattern repeats for `get_memory_info()` — each call makes its own Redis round trip per buffer. Consumers with many shards and `max_processes` set high now perform N Redis calls (record_stored_segments, plus N more for memory info when memory backpressure is enabled) per submit where the accepted design performed one, reintroducing per-message Redis latency that the original single-buffer design explicitly avoided.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `SpanFlusher.submit()` changed from a single `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()` call to a loop over `self.buffers.values()` calling `record_stored_segments()` per buffer, and similarly changed memory backpressure from `list(self.buffer.get_memory_info())` to iterating all buffers and extending `memory_infos` with each `buffer.get_memory_info()` (see `submit()` in `flusher.py`). Since `self.buffers` are newly created as separate `SpansBuffer(shards)` instances per process (`_create_process_for_shards`), this increases the number of buffer method invocations per submit from 1 to `num_processes` (which can equal shard count when `max_processes` is high). The claim about Redis round trips is plausible given the flusher/buffer context but is not directly verifiable from this diff alone; what is verifiable is the new O(num_processes) pattern on every submit, which can reintroduce per-submit latency/overhead compared to the prior single-buffer approach.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test was changed from `@pytest.mark.django_db` to `@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)` and an unconditional `time.sleep(0.1)` was added after a bare `step.poll()` with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' — a test-only accommodation of the new multi-thread timing that the original synchronous-flush test did not need. The test now asserts the end-to-end message contents after a fixed 100ms sleep against background flusher threads, so CI intermittently fails (or silently passes with partially-flushed state) whenever thread scheduling exceeds the sleep; the next engineer debugging this flake cannot tell whether the flusher is broken or the sleep is too short, and the drift-change accompaniment masks real ordering regressions.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add `@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)` and a `time.sleep(0.1)` after `step.poll()` in `test_basic`, but the test also immediately monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so that `time.sleep(0.1)` is not an actual 100ms wait and is not “asserting after a fixed 100ms sleep”. The claim about CI intermittently failing due to the 100ms sleep and thread scheduling is not verifiable from the diff (and the sleep is effectively a no-op here).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The added `time.sleep(0.1)` in test_basic is a no-op because the same test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at its start, so the 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' wait never actually waits. The fix for the drift-change race is illusory: the flusher threads get zero wall-clock time before step.join(), so the test still races with the background threads and intermittently fails or (worse) passes without actually exercising the post-drift flush, giving false confidence that the timing change was tested.
matched_golden_ids: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate explicitly notes that test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op (lambda _: None), so the later time.sleep(0.1) call does not actually wait. This is the same underlying issue described in the golden comment: the test expects a real delay but sleep has been monkeypatched to return immediately.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts internal bookkeeping (`len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes == 2`, `num_processes == 2`, shard-count sum) and never verifies that the two processes actually flush the data assigned to their shards. A regression where per-shard buffers are mis-wired (e.g. the round-robin process_to_shards_map assigns a shard to a process whose SpansBuffer(shards) excludes it, or a shared process never polls its second shard's Redis keys) passes this test, because no message flows through any of the 4 partitions — the test is a mirror of the constructor's arithmetic, not of flushing behavior. I checked tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py and test_flusher.py: neither asserts per-process or per-shard output when flusher_processes < shard count.

adjudication.rationale: In `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py`, `test_flusher_processes_limit` only checks internal state (`len(flusher.processes)`, `max_processes`, `num_processes`, and that `process_to_shards_map` covers 4 shards) and then immediately `step.join()` without ever submitting messages or asserting any flushed/produced output for any shard. Given the new logic in `SpanFlusher` that creates per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` and maps shards round-robin (`process_to_shards_map` + `_create_process_for_shards`), a wiring/regression where a process doesn’t actually flush one of its assigned shards would not be caught by this test. This is a specific, diff-grounded gap in coverage of the newly added multi-process/shard-sharing behavior, not a demonstrated production defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] test_flusher_processes_limit ends with a bare `step.join()` and never asserts any flushed messages or commits, so it cannot detect that the 2 shared processes fail to produce the segments written by submit(). If the refactor from one buffer to N per-shard SpansBuffer instances breaks data flow for shared processes (e.g. record_stored_segments on shard buffers that the flusher processes never read), the test still passes green, shipping a silent data-loss regression in span ingestion. The `messages` list captured via produce_to_pipe is never inspected.

adjudication.rationale: In `test_flusher_processes_limit`, the diff shows it only creates the strategy, asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes/num_processes == 2`, and checks shard distribution, then calls `step.join()`—it never calls `step.submit(...)` and never inspects `messages` or `commits`. So the test only verifies process/shard mapping, not end-to-end flushing/producing behavior under shared processes, meaning a data-flow regression could slip by undetected. This is a concrete gap in the added test rather than a verifiable functional bug by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new restart/health logic in _ensure_processes_alive (per-process hang detection via process_healthy_since, process crash via is_alive/exitcode, the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError, and the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)-guarded kill) has no test in this diff that triggers any of these branches — both modified test files (test_consumer.py, test_flusher.py) only exercise the happy healthy path. The most safety-critical behavioral changes of the PR — kill/restart of a shared process, the AttributeError catch on killing a threading.Thread path, and the repeated-crash consumer restart — are unverified; a bug there (e.g. restart counter reset, wrong shared-state Value passed on recreate) ships silently and only surfaces as a hung or crash-looping production consumer.

adjudication.rationale: The diff substantially changes SpanFlusher lifecycle logic from a single process to multiple processes with per-process health/backpressure tracking and restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive()` (e.g., `not process.is_alive()`, hang detection via `process_healthy_since[...]`, per-process `process_restarts[...] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` RuntimeError, and guarded `process.kill()` only for `multiprocessing.Process` with `(ValueError, AttributeError)` handling). The modified/added tests (`test_basic`, `test_flusher_processes_limit`, and `test_flusher` change) only validate normal initialization/happy-path behavior (process count/shard distribution, backpressure value presence) and do not trigger any unhealthy branches or restart behavior. That is a concrete, diff-grounded gap in coverage for newly added safety-critical behavior, not itself a proven defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The assertion was weakened from a specific `flusher.backpressure_since.value` check to `any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())`, which passes when only one of several per-process backpressure flags is set. In this multiprocess design the test now masks the case where some shard-processes never register backpressure that the old single-process code would have caught (e.g. a shared process whose backpressure Value is mis-wired in _create_process_for_shards); the test also never asserts the process_backpressure_since values belong to the processes actually owning the shards under load.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does weaken the test in `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py` from asserting a single `backpressure_since.value` to `any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())`. Given the new design introduces multiple per-process backpressure flags (`process_backpressure_since` dict in `SpanFlusher.__init__`), asserting `any(...)` only verifies that at least one worker observed backpressure and does not exercise/validate correct wiring or behavior across all processes/shard assignments (e.g., each process index has its own `Value` passed into `SpanFlusher.main`). This is a test-coverage weakness rather than a verifiable runtime defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] A hung flusher running as a threading.Thread (the produce_to_pipe/test path) is never terminated on restart, so a duplicate flusher thread polls the same shards as the freshly spawned replacement. When the 'hang' path fires for a thread-based flusher, the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard skips the kill, _create_process_for_shards starts a second thread over the same shards; if the hung thread recovers, both threads consume the same Redis segments and produce duplicate span payloads to Kafka.

adjudication.rationale: In the produce_to_pipe path, SpanFlusher uses threading.Thread (see _create_process_for_shards: make_process = threading.Thread when self.produce_to_pipe is not None). In _ensure_processes_alive, on hang/no_process it attempts to stop the unhealthy worker only via `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()`, so threads are never terminated. It then unconditionally calls `_create_process_for_shards(...)`, which starts a new thread for the same shard set and overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` without stopping the old thread. If the old hung thread later resumes, both threads would poll/flush the same shards and can produce duplicate payloads. join() similarly only terminates multiprocessing.Process instances, not threads.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] max_processes uses `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so flusher_processes=0 (or any falsy value) silently expands to one process per shard instead of being rejected or clamped. An operator setting --flusher-processes 0 via the new click option gets the maximum process count on a consumer with thousands of shards, multiplying spawn/Redis connection load with no error signal; the config value is silently ignored rather than validated.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` means a provided falsy value like `0` will be treated as “unset” and replaced with `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. With the new `--flusher-processes` click option (`type=int` with no validation), an operator can pass `0` and unintentionally spawn one process per shard (`self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))`), silently ignoring the configured limit and potentially causing excessive process/Redis load.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code (no call sites in the diff) and, if ever wired up, would spawn a new process for a shard's group without killing the existing process stored in self.processes[process_index], leaking a live process that still flushes those shards. The next maintainer who fixes a rebalance bug by calling this method gets overlapping processes double-flushing the same shards; the deletion test passes — removing the method removes a future duplicate-data hazard.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `SpanFlusher` defines `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` but there are no call sites added/changed that invoke it, so it is currently dead code. The method calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` without first killing/terminating the existing `processes[process_index]` entry, unlike `_ensure_processes_alive` which explicitly kills the old process before recreating it. If a future maintainer wires `_create_process_for_shard` into rebalance handling, it could spawn an additional process/thread for the same shard set and leave the old one running, creating overlapping flushers. That’s a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability/future-safety issue, but not a presently verifiable runtime defect given the method is unused in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats an explicit `flusher_processes=0` as unset and silently falls back to one process per shard. An operator who sets --flusher-processes 0 intending to disable/limit the flusher instead gets the maximum fan-out (one spawn process per shard), the exact opposite of the requested limit, with no warning logged.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, the diff sets `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. This means an explicitly provided `max_processes=0` (plausible via the new `--flusher-processes` click option, which is `type=int` with no lower-bound validation) will be treated as falsy and replaced with `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, resulting in maximal fan-out rather than the requested limit. The diff shows no validation or error/logging for `0`, so the finding is a real behavior defect introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When a hung flusher is running as a threading.Thread (produce_to_pipe mode), the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard means the hung thread is never killed before a replacement thread is spawned for the same shards. Two threads concurrently flush the same Redis shards, producing duplicate span batches to Kafka while the health monitor reports the flusher as recovered — silent data duplication with no error surfaced.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive`, when a flusher is deemed unhealthy it attempts to stop the old worker before calling `self._create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. However, the stop logic only runs `process.kill()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. In `produce_to_pipe` mode, the worker is created as a `threading.Thread` (see `_create_process_for_shards`: `make_process = threading.Thread`), so the unhealthy (hung) thread is not killed/terminated/joined and a replacement thread is spawned for the same `shards`. Because both threads are constructed with `SpansBuffer(shards)` and will poll/flush the same Redis shards, this can plausibly lead to concurrent double-flushing/duplicate production while the health metric appears recovered (new thread updates `healthy_since`). This behavior is directly implied by the diff: replacement without any thread-stopping mechanism beyond the no-op guard.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] In join(), once the deadline is exhausted the `break` skips the terminate() call for all not-yet-iterated processes, leaving spawned flusher processes running past the consumer shutdown deadline. During a slow shutdown with a short join timeout, multiple non-daemon-joined flusher processes linger and keep polling Redis/producing to Kafka while the consumer is reported as shut down; behavior gets worse as flusher_processes grows since each process gets a fresh slice of the deadline.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.join()`, the loop over `self.processes` does `if remaining_time <= 0: break` before reaching the per-process `terminate()` call. This means once the global `deadline` is exceeded, any not-yet-iterated multiprocessing flusher processes are neither waited on nor terminated and can continue running after shutdown (despite `self.stopped.value = True`). This behavior is directly visible in the new join logic added in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] When flusher_processes is None (any programmatic caller of ProcessSpansStrategyFactory that doesn't pass the new kwarg), the default silently changes from 1 shared flusher process to one process per shard. Any existing deployment/tooling that constructs the factory without --flusher-processes via the click option (tests, internal scripts) now spawns len(assigned_shards) processes instead of 1, multiplying Redis connections and memory with no operator action.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does change the default behavior for programmatic callers: `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` adds `flusher_processes: int | None = None` and passes it to `SpanFlusher(..., max_processes=self.flusher_processes)`. In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` so `None` results in `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, and `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` yields one process/thread per shard. Previously there was a single background process/thread handling all shards. This is a real, diff-grounded operational/behavior change (and inconsistent with the Click option defaulting to 1), but it’s not a clear correctness defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The metrics timers use inconsistent tag keys: 'shard' for spans.buffer.flusher.produce and segment_size_bytes, but 'shards' for spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce. Anyone debugging shard-level flusher latency in the metrics dashboard cannot join wait_produce with produce/segment_size metrics — the tag mismatch silently splits the series and misdirects investigation of slow flushes.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py`, the diff introduces shard tagging as `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` for `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`, but uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` for `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`. This is a real, diff-grounded observability issue: the same shard identifier will be split across different tag keys, making dashboards/queries unable to correlate wait vs produce timings by shard.
